readings.title: The Small Gap Before a Screen
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
At the end of each shift, Mara took the tram home and opened her phone before she had found a seat. She intended to check the next day's weather. Twenty minutes later, she would look up and realize that she had read messages, viewed short videos, and almost missed her stop. None of these activities was terrible by itself. What troubled her was how little she remembered choosing to do them.

Mara tried leaving the phone in her bag for the entire journey. This worked for two days, then failed when she needed to tell a friend that the tram was late. A more useful change came from a question: what was the phone for at this moment? Before unlocking it, she began to name a purpose, such as “send one message” or “check the weather.” Once she had done that task, she put the phone away. Sometimes she still watched a video, but she decided to do so rather than arriving there by accident.

She also changed the first screen of her phone. Weather, maps, and messages remained easy to find; entertainment apps moved into a folder on the second page. The extra second required to open the folder was not a barrier. It was a small gap in which she could ask herself whether she wanted a break or was simply responding to a bright icon.

Her colleague Ben thought the method sounded too simple to matter. Yet he noticed a similar pattern at work. While writing a report, he repeatedly checked a group chat because its symbol showed an unread message. He turned off that symbol during two morning hours, then checked the chat at a planned time. He still answered important requests, and his report no longer had to be restarted every few minutes.

Neither Mara nor Ben concluded that attention could be protected by a single rule. Their needs differed from day to day. Their shared lesson was that a brief pause can turn a habit into a choice. The goal was to use a screen for a purpose, including enjoyment, while keeping enough room to notice what that purpose was.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：数字习惯与注意力

readings.title: A Warm Room, Not a Warm House
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When the Han family received a larger winter energy bill, they first considered replacing every appliance. Their neighbour, who repaired buildings, suggested a smaller experiment. For one week they would record when each room was used and how warm it needed to be. The kitchen was busy in the morning, the living room in the evening, and two bedrooms were empty most of the day.

The family kept the shared living room comfortable in the evening but turned down heat in unused rooms. They closed the living-room door when it was occupied and opened curtains during sunny hours. Their first surprise was that the old curtain in a bedroom mattered more than they expected: a cold draft crossed the desk each night. A thicker curtain reduced the draft, although it did not solve every problem. They also checked that a shelf was not blocking a heater.

Their teenage son proposed running the washing machine only at night, after hearing that electricity could cost less then. His parents checked the bill carefully. Their plan charged the same price at all hours, so changing the time would not lower the charge. They still chose full loads rather than several half loads, because this reduced the number of cycles.

At the end of the month, the family had used less energy, but they were cautious about the comparison. The weather had become milder, which could also explain part of the change. They planned to compare similar weeks and keep notes about comfort as well as cost. If the bedrooms became too cold for sleep, the plan would need changing. Saving energy was useful only if the home remained healthy and workable.

The experiment did not produce one dramatic purchase. Instead, it gave the family a way to make decisions: observe where energy was needed, check claims against the actual payment plan, and revise small changes in light of results. This approach made the bill less mysterious and helped them choose which future repairs deserved attention.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：家庭能源选择与证据判断

readings.title: The Recipe on Two Screens
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
When Mei asked her grandfather Jun for the recipe for his tomato noodles, he laughed. “I never wrote one,” he said. He cooked by looking at the colour of the sauce and tasting it. Mei, who had learned many dishes from short online videos, wanted exact amounts. Their first attempt to cook together was awkward. She held up her phone to record each step, while he moved quickly and forgot to say what he had just added.

The following Saturday, Mei changed her plan. She placed the phone on a shelf and asked only one question at a time. Jun slowed down enough to explain why he warmed the pan before adding the tomatoes. Mei measured the ingredients as he used them, but she also wrote his descriptions: “soft enough to crush with a spoon” and “a little sharper than you want the final sauce.”

Jun was curious about the video Mei made. He had assumed that sharing a recipe online meant showing a perfect performance. Mei showed him a clip in which a cook admitted that a sauce was too thin and demonstrated how to fix it. Jun said that was the part he would have watched. He then asked Mei to include their own mistake: they had added salt twice and used another tomato to restore the balance.

When Mei edited the recording, she did not present Jun as a person who knew nothing about digital tools. Nor did she claim that measuring would replace his judgement. She added captions for the amounts and left in his advice about colour and taste. Jun checked the captions because one spoonful had been labelled as two. In return, he asked Mei to show him how to pause and replay a video without losing his place.

The finished recipe did not settle which way of learning was better. A viewer could follow the measurements, notice the changing sauce, and see that a mistake could be repaired. More importantly for Mei and Jun, the project gave them a reason to ask questions they had stopped asking each other. Their different habits became materials for a shared task instead of reasons to give up the conversation.

readings.title: The Question After the Demonstration
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
On her first week at a repair workshop, Salma watched an experienced technician, Owen, test a small water pump. He named each tool and completed the work neatly. When Salma tried the same task, she followed the written steps but missed a faint leak near a joint. Owen pointed it out and repeated the demonstration. The second attempt was little better. Salma could copy his actions, yet she did not know what he was noticing.

Before the next repair, Owen changed his approach. He asked Salma to predict where a leak would be most likely and why. She pointed to a damaged hose, which was a reasonable guess. Owen then explained that the hose was dry but the joint showed a thin line of moisture. He invited her to describe the evidence before either of them touched the pump. By giving her time to state her reasoning, he could see which part of the problem she understood.

Owen also began keeping a short record with Salma after each job. They wrote down the symptom, the first guess, what they observed, and the final repair. The record was not a list of her errors. Sometimes Owen's first guess was wrong too, and he included it. This made it easier for Salma to ask questions without worrying that uncertainty would be taken as carelessness.

After several weeks, Salma noticed a soft change in the sound of another pump. She stopped the test and asked Owen whether it might mean air was entering the system. It did not; a loose cover was vibrating. Even so, Owen praised the decision to stop and investigate. In their workshop, an early question was safer than a confident guess that went unexamined.

By the end of the month, Salma still needed guidance on unfamiliar machines, but her questions had become more precise. Owen had learned something as well: showing a skilled action was only the beginning of teaching it. A mentor could make experience visible by asking for predictions, discussing evidence, and treating corrected guesses as useful steps toward independent judgement.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese.

A useful habit often begins with a small observation. Before changing a routine, we can ask when a problem appears and what conditions make it worse. A family trying to use less energy, for example, may discover that one room is heated long after everyone has left it. They can then adjust that room rather than making the whole house uncomfortable. The first change may not produce a clear result, because weather and daily schedules also affect energy use. Keeping simple notes helps people compare similar days and decide whether to continue. This patient approach applies beyond the home: when we understand a situation before acting, even a modest change is more likely to be useful.
knowledgePoints: 英译汉：语义与逻辑关系
translation.explanation: 仅供考生自评。注意before引导的时间关系、rather than的对比、because解释结果不明的原因，以及beyond the home所表达的适用范围。按意义完整、语言准确和表达自然评分。
translation.referenceAnswer: 一种有用的习惯往往始于细小的观察。改变日常做法之前，我们可以先问问问题何时出现，以及什么条件会使它变得更严重。例如，一个希望减少能源使用的家庭可能发现，所有人离开某个房间很久后，那里仍在供暖。于是，他们可以调整这个房间的供暖，而不必让整栋房子都变得不舒适。第一次调整未必会产生明确的结果，因为天气和每天的作息也会影响能源使用。做些简单记录，有助于人们比较条件相近的日子，并决定是否继续采用这一做法。这种耐心的方法并不只适用于家庭：当我们在行动前先了解情况时，即使是适度的改变，也更有可能发挥作用。

criteria.name: 意义完整
criteria.description: 准确传达主要信息、例证及因果和对比关系，不遗漏关键内容。

criteria.name: 语言准确
criteria.description: 词义、时态、指代与句间逻辑处理准确，避免明显误译。

criteria.name: 表达自然
criteria.description: 中文流畅，句子衔接清楚，符合书面表达习惯。

writing.stem:
Write at least 100 words in English on the following topic: A Practical Change to Improve Daily Attention.

Your adult learning centre has invited students to share one realistic way to reduce unnecessary interruptions during study or work. Write a short article for its newsletter. Describe a situation in which attention is often lost, explain one specific change you would try, and discuss how you would judge whether the change is helpful. Mention one limitation or adjustment. You may use an imagined example. Do not write your real name or contact details.
knowledgePoints: 写作：建议、评估与连贯表达
writing.explanation: 仅供考生自评。范文描述学习时查看手机的干扰，提出具体设置和检查时间，说明评估方法及调整余地。评分看要点覆盖、组织连贯和语言运用，不要求照搬范文。
writing.sampleAnswer:
When I study after work, a message notification can make me lose my place in a difficult paragraph. I may spend only a minute replying, but returning to the text takes much longer. I would therefore silence ordinary app alerts for a forty-minute study period. Calls from my family would remain available, and I would check messages during a ten-minute break.

To judge whether this change helps, I would note how many pages I understand and how often I have to reread a section. I would compare several evenings with similar study tasks instead of relying on one unusually quiet day. If forty minutes feels too long, I could begin with twenty-five. The purpose is to make my attention more deliberate, not to ignore people who may need me.

criteria.name: 任务完成
criteria.description: 写明注意力流失的情境、具体改变、评估办法及限制或调整。

criteria.name: 组织连贯
criteria.description: 结构清晰，段落和衔接自然，符合简短文章的体裁。

criteria.name: 语言运用
criteria.description: 词汇、语法基本准确，句式有适当变化，表达清楚。
